The full spec is below — it is final. Probe every spec line with a test a plausible wrong implementation would fail (e.g. inherited props like toString/__proto__/constructor must be "not found"; `__proto__` member added as own property; index tokens 01,+1,1.0,1e0," 1",length,"" → bad index; "-" on array → path not found (not bad index) when following; add with index > length → path not found; -0 preserved in copies; member order (adding /1 to {"b":0} gives {"1":5,"b":0}); doc and patch unchanged even when throwing; result shares no object with inputs; form-check of ALL ops before applying any; holes in patch = not an object; String object op = bad op; non-enumerable own `op` counts; move same from/path no-op only after from found; move index counted after removal; copy into own child; test equality 0 vs -0, 1 vs 1.0, object key order, no Unicode normalization; error index; CLI order of checks (patch fully validated before doc is read — e.g. bad patch JSON + missing doc file → patch error), BOM, invalid UTF-8, too large counting bytes read (1048576 OK, 1048577 too large incl BOM), too deep at 1001 vs 1000 OK, directory, ENOTDIR (file/x), usage cases ("-" alone, "- -", 0 or 3 args), exit codes, stdout empty on error, stderr empty on success). If you find a case where the implementation violates the spec, do not change the implementation: report it to me (main) in your REPORT with the failing test and spec line, and leave the test in place.

Done means: tests in test/ cover the spec, `npm test` run, results reported (pass/fail with details of any spec violations found).

=== SPEC ===
Build a JSON Patch library `jsonpatch.mjs` (an ES module with the named exports `parsePointer`, `applyPatch` and `PatchError`; no default export is needed) and a command-line tool `jsonpatch-cli.mjs` (an ES module, run as `node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]`) that applies a patch to a JSON document. Put both files at the project root, next to `package.json`. The rules follow JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) and JSON Patch (RFC 6902); where this text is more exact, this text wins. Throughout, a "string" is a primitive string, a value whose `typeof` is `'string'`; a String object such as `new String('/a')` is not a string.

Pointers
- A valid pointer is the empty string, or `/` followed by reference tokens separated by `/`: "" has no tokens, "/" has one token (the empty string), and "/a//b/" has the tokens "a", "", "b" and "".
- In a token, `~1` stands for `/` and `~0` for `~`, so "/~01" has the token "~1" and "/~10" has the token "/0". A `~` that is not followed by `0` or `1`, or a non-empty string that does not start with `/`, makes the pointer invalid.
- `parsePointer(pointer)` returns a new array of the decoded tokens. A pointer that is not a string (a String object included): throw a `TypeError` with the message `pointer must be a string`. An invalid pointer: throw a `SyntaxError` with the message `invalid pointer`.
- A pointer is followed token by token, starting at the whole document:
  - On an object, a token names the object's own member of exactly that name, if it has one. `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString` and every other name are ordinary member names: inherited properties never count.
  - On an array, a token that is `0`, or a digit 1-9 followed by any digits, is an index: it names the element at that index when the index is less than the array's length. `-` names no element. Any other token (for example `01`, `+1`, `1.0`, `1e0`, ` 1`, `length` or "") is a bad index.
  - On a string, number, boolean or null, no token names anything.

Patches
- `applyPatch(doc, patch)` returns the document that results from applying `patch` to `doc`. `doc` is a JSON value as `JSON.parse` returns it. `patch`, each element of it and each member of an operation may be any JavaScript value, except that the `value` member of an `add`, `replace` or `test`, when present, is a JSON value as `JSON.parse` returns it (never undefined). No getter, setter or Proxy appears anywhere in `doc` or `patch`, so any property may be read any number of times. The tests never pass a `doc` or a `value` more than 1000 levels deep (depth as defined under Command line).
- `applyPatch` never changes `doc` or `patch`, also when it throws, and the value it returns shares no object or array with them (a patch of `[]` returns a deep copy of `doc`). Every copy, including each `value` that `add`, `replace` or `copy` puts into the result, keeps every number exactly as it is, -0 included (a patch of `[]` on `{"a":-0}` returns `{a: -0}`), and keeps member order.
- Member order is JavaScript's own property order, as `Object.keys` gives it: names that are array indices ("0" to "4294967294", written without leading zeros) come first in ascending numeric order, then the other names in the order they were added. So a new name goes last among the names of its kind: adding `/1` with value 5 to `{"b":0}` gives `{"1":5,"b":0}`, and the command line prints it in that order.
- `patch` must be an array, as `Array.isArray` decides. Every index from 0 to `patch.length - 1` holds an operation; a hole counts as the value undefined. First every operation is checked, in order, against the form rules below; the first one that breaks them stops `applyPatch` before anything is applied. Then the operations are applied in order, each to the result of the one before; the first one that fails stops `applyPatch`.
- An operation has a member `name` when `Object.hasOwn(op, name)` is true, whether or not the property is enumerable; inherited properties never count. Members that its `op` does not use are ignored, whatever their value (for example `from` on an `add`, or `value` on a `remove`).

Form rules (the reason is the first of these that applies to the operation)
- `not an object`: the operation is null, an array, or a value whose `typeof` is not `'object'`. So a function or a hole is `not an object`, while a String object, a Date or any other object goes on to the next rule.
- `bad op`: `op` is missing, or is not exactly (`===`) one of the strings `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`.
- `bad path`: `path` is missing, is not a string, or is not a valid pointer.
- `bad from`: for `move` and `copy`, `from` is missing, is not a string, or is not a valid pointer.
- `missing value`: for `add`, `replace` and `test`, there is no `value` member (a `value` of null is present).
- `cannot remove root`: a `remove` whose `path` is "".
- `cannot move into own child`: a `move` whose `from` tokens are a proper prefix of its `path` tokens. A `from` of "" is a proper prefix of every other path; `/a` is not a prefix of `/ab`.

Operations
- `add`: a `path` of "" makes `value` the whole document. Otherwise the tokens of `path` but the last are followed to the parent. On an object, the last token is the member name: a name the object does not have becomes a new own member of it (placed as the member order rule says), and an existing member gets `value` and keeps its place. On an array, `-` appends `value`, and an index up to and including the array's length inserts `value` at that index, moving the later elements up.
- `remove`: `path` must name a value, which is removed (from an array, the later elements move down).
- `replace`: a `path` of "" makes `value` the whole document. Otherwise `path` must name a value, which becomes `value`; a member keeps its place.
- `move`: `from` must name a value. It is removed as `remove` does, then added at `path` as `add` does, so an array index in `path` counts after the removal. A `move` whose `from` equals its `path` leaves the document as it is (once `from` is found).
- `copy`: `from` must name a value. A deep copy of it, taken before anything changes, is added at `path` as `add` does; `path` may lie inside `from`.
- `test`: `path` must name a value ("" names the whole document), and that value must equal `value`: both are the same JSON type, and numbers have the same value (1, 1.0 and 1e0 are equal, and so are 0 and -0); strings have exactly the same characters (no Unicode normalization); arrays have the same length and equal elements in the same order; objects have the same member names, in any order, with equal values; true, false and null equal only themselves.

Failures while applying
- The first token of a pointer that names nothing stops the operation: with `bad index` if it is a bad index on an array, otherwise with `from not found` while following `from` and `path not found` while following `path`. `move` and `copy` follow `from` first.
- `add` follows only the parent; its last token then fails with `path not found` when the parent is neither an object nor an array, or is an array and the token is an index greater than the array's length, and with `bad index` when the parent is an array and the token is neither `-` nor an index.
- `test failed`: the value at `path` does not equal `value`.

Errors
- `PatchError` is a subclass of `Error` whose `name` is `PatchError`, and each one `applyPatch` throws has an `index` property. `applyPatch` throws nothing else. The tests never construct a `PatchError` themselves; they check only `instanceof PatchError`, `instanceof Error`, `name`, `message` and `index` on the errors `applyPatch` throws.
- When `patch` is not an array, the message is `patch must be an array` and `index` is null. Otherwise the message is `operation <i>: <reason>` and `index` is the number `<i>`, the 0-based position of the failing operation in `patch` (for example `operation 2: test failed`).

Command line
- `node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]` reads the patch from the file `<patch>` and the document from the file `<doc>`. A missing `<doc>`, or an argument that is exactly `-`, means standard input. Every other argument is a file path.
- On success, write `JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)` followed by "\n" to stdout, write nothing to stderr, and exit 0.
- Each input is read as UTF-8; a byte order mark (U+FEFF) at its very start is ignored. The text is then parsed as `JSON.parse` does.
- The steps run in this order, and the first one that fails is reported: the arguments; the patch input (read, then decoded, then parsed, then checked for depth); the document input (the same four steps); applying the patch. So the document input is not read until the patch input has passed every check.

Errors (exactly one line to stderr, ending in "\n"; nothing to stdout). `<name>` is the argument as given, or `stdin` for standard input.
- Not 1 or 2 arguments, or both inputs are standard input: `Usage: node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]`, exit 2.
- Read errors exit 1, and the reason is the first of these that applies. `Error: <name>: no such file`: no file system entry exists at the path, so opening it fails with ENOENT or ENOTDIR (for example `nope.json`, or `patch.json/x` where `patch.json` is a regular file; the tests never put a trailing `/` after a regular file's name). `Error: <name>: is a directory`: the path names a directory, whatever its permissions. `Error: <name>: too large`: more than 1048576 bytes (a byte order mark included) were read from the input; this counts the bytes actually read, not the size the file system reports, so a file that cannot be opened is `cannot read` whatever its size. `Error: <name>: cannot read`: any other read error. For standard input only `too large` and `cannot read` apply.
- Bytes that are not valid UTF-8: `Error: <name>: invalid UTF-8`. Text that `JSON.parse` rejects, an empty input included: `Error: <name>: invalid JSON`. A JSON value nested more than 1000 levels deep: `Error: <name>: too deep`, where a string, number, boolean or null has depth 0 and an array or object has depth one more than the deepest value in it (so `[]` and `{}` have depth 1). Each exits 3.
- `applyPatch` throws a `PatchError`: `Error: <message>` (for example `Error: operation 0: bad op`), exit 4.

Also add tests with node:test, a `package.json` ("type": "module" and a "test" script), and a README with usage.
=== END SPEC ===

# jsonpatch

A dependency-free JSON Pointer ([RFC 6901](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901)) and
JSON Patch ([RFC 6902](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6902)) library and command-line tool
for Node.js (ES modules, Node 18+).

## Library

```js
import { parsePointer, applyPatch, PatchError } from './jsonpatch.mjs';

parsePointer('/a~1b/~0c/0'); // ['a/b', '~c', '0']

const doc = { name: 'x', tags: ['a'] };
const result = applyPatch(doc, [
  { op: 'add', path: '/tags/-', value: 'b' },
  { op: 'replace', path: '/name', value: 'y' },
  { op: 'test', path: '/tags/0', value: 'a' },
]);
// result: { name: 'y', tags: ['a', 'b'] }; doc is unchanged
```

- `parsePointer(pointer)` returns the decoded reference tokens. It throws a `TypeError`
  (`pointer must be a string`) for a non-string and a `SyntaxError` (`invalid pointer`) for an
  invalid pointer.
- `applyPatch(doc, patch)` returns a new document. It never changes `doc` or `patch`, and the
  result shares no objects or arrays with them. Every operation is checked for form before any is
  applied; the first failure throws a `PatchError`.
- `PatchError` has `name` `'PatchError'`, a `message` such as `operation 2: test failed`, and an
  `index` (the 0-based position of the failing operation, or `null` when `patch` is not an array).

Failure reasons: `not an object`, `bad op`, `bad path`, `bad from`, `missing value`,
`cannot remove root`, `cannot move into own child`, `path not found`, `from not found`,
`bad index`, `test failed`.

## Command line

```sh
node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]
```

Reads the patch from the file `<patch>` and the document from `<doc>`. A missing `<doc>`, or an
argument of `-`, means standard input (only one input may be standard input). On success the
result is printed as 2-space indented JSON.

```sh
echo '{"a":1}' | node jsonpatch-cli.mjs patch.json
node jsonpatch-cli.mjs patch.json doc.json
```

Build a JSON Patch library `jsonpatch.mjs` (named exports `parsePointer`, `applyPatch`, `PatchError`) and a CLI `jsonpatch-cli.mjs` (run as `node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]`). "string" = primitive string (typeof 'string'); a String object such as `new String('/a')` is not a string.

Pointers
- A valid pointer is "", or `/` followed by reference tokens separated by `/`: "" has no tokens, "/" has one token (""), "/a//b/" has tokens "a","","b","".
- In a token `~1` -> `/`, `~0` -> `~`, so "/~01" has token "~1" and "/~10" has token "/0". A `~` not followed by 0 or 1, or a non-empty string not starting with `/`, is invalid.
- parsePointer(pointer) returns a new array of decoded tokens. Not a string (String object included): throw TypeError message `pointer must be a string`. Invalid: throw SyntaxError message `invalid pointer`.
- Following, token by token from the whole document:
  - Object: token names the object's OWN member of exactly that name. `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString` etc. are ordinary names; inherited properties never count.
  - Array: token `0` or digit 1-9 followed by digits is an index; names the element when index < length. `-` names no element. Any other token (`01`, `+1`, `1.0`, `1e0`, ` 1`, `length`, "") is a bad index.
  - string/number/boolean/null: no token names anything.

Patches
- applyPatch(doc, patch) returns the result. doc is a JSON value as JSON.parse returns. patch/elements/members may be any JS value, except `value` of add/replace/test when present is a JSON value.
- applyPatch never changes doc or patch, also when it throws, and the result shares no object/array with them (patch [] returns a deep copy). Every copy (incl. each value add/replace/copy put in) keeps numbers exactly, -0 included ([] on {"a":-0} returns {a:-0}), and keeps member order.
- Member order = Object.keys order: array-index names ascending first, then others in insertion order. Adding /1 value 5 to {"b":0} gives {"1":5,"b":0}; CLI prints in that order.
- patch must be an array (Array.isArray). Each index 0..length-1 holds an op; a hole is undefined. FIRST every op is form-checked in order; first failure stops before anything is applied. THEN ops applied in order; first failure stops.
- An op has member `name` when Object.hasOwn(op, name), enumerable or not; inherited never count. Unused members ignored whatever their value (`from` on add, `value` on remove).

Form rules (reason = first that applies)
- `not an object`: null, an array, or typeof not 'object'. Function or hole -> not an object; String object, Date, other objects go on.
- `bad op`: op missing or not === one of add, remove, replace, move, copy, test.
- `bad path`: path missing, not a string, or invalid pointer.
- `bad from`: for move and copy, from missing/not string/invalid.
- `missing value`: for add, replace, test, no `value` member (value null is present).
- `cannot remove root`: remove with path "".
- `cannot move into own child`: move whose from tokens are a PROPER prefix of path tokens. from "" is a proper prefix of every other path; /a is not prefix of /ab.

Operations
- add: path "" makes value the whole doc. Else follow all tokens but last to the parent. Object: new name becomes new own member (placed per member order); existing member gets value and keeps its place. Array: `-` appends; index <= length inserts at that index, shifting later elements up.
- remove: path must name a value; removed (array: later elements move down).
- replace: path "" -> value becomes whole doc. Else path must name a value, which becomes value; member keeps its place.
- move: from must name a value. Removed as remove does, then added at path as add does, so an array index in path counts after the removal. move with from equal to path leaves doc as is (once from is found).
- copy: from must name a value. Deep copy taken before anything changes, added at path as add does; path may lie inside from.
- test: path must name a value ("" = whole doc), equal to value: same JSON type; numbers same value (1, 1.0, 1e0 equal; 0 and -0 equal); strings exactly same chars (no Unicode normalization); arrays same length, equal elements in order; objects same member names in any order with equal values; true/false/null only equal themselves.

Failures while applying
- First token of a pointer that names nothing stops the op: `bad index` if a bad index on an array, else `from not found` while following from, `path not found` while following path. move and copy follow from first.
- add follows only the parent; its last token fails with `path not found` when parent is neither object nor array, or is an array and token is an index > length; and `bad index` when parent is an array and token is neither `-` nor an index.
- `test failed`: value at path not equal.

Errors
- PatchError subclass of Error, name 'PatchError', each thrown has `index`. applyPatch throws nothing else. Check instanceof PatchError, instanceof Error, name, message, index.
- patch not an array: message `patch must be an array`, index null. Else message `operation <i>: <reason>`, index the number i.

Command line
- `node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]` reads patch from file <patch> and doc from file <doc>. Missing <doc>, or an argument exactly `-`, means stdin. Every other argument is a file path.
- Success: stdout = JSON.stringify(result, null, 2) + "\n", nothing on stderr, exit 0.
- Inputs read as UTF-8; a BOM (U+FEFF) at the very start is ignored. Then parsed as JSON.parse.
- Order (first failure reported): the arguments; the patch input (read, decode, parse, depth check); the doc input (same four); applying. The doc input is not read until the patch passed every check.

CLI errors (exactly one line to stderr ending "\n"; stdout empty). <name> is the argument as given, or `stdin`.
- Not 1 or 2 args, or both inputs stdin: `Usage: node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]`, exit 2.
- Read errors exit 1, first that applies: `Error: <name>: no such file` (open fails ENOENT or ENOTDIR, e.g. `nope.json` or `patch.json/x` where patch.json is a regular file). `Error: <name>: is a directory`. `Error: <name>: too large`: more than 1048576 bytes (BOM included) read; counts bytes actually read. `Error: <name>: cannot read`: any other read error. For stdin only too large and cannot read apply.
- `Error: <name>: invalid UTF-8`; `Error: <name>: invalid JSON` (empty input included); `Error: <name>: too deep` (value nested > 1000 levels; primitives depth 0, [] and {} depth 1). Each exit 3.
- applyPatch throws PatchError: `Error: <message>` (e.g. `Error: operation 0: bad op`), exit 4.
EOF
